items.title: Emergence of the Pallavas of Kanchi
items.body:
## Rise of the Imperial Pallavas

- The Pallavas rose to prominence after **Simhavishnu defeated the Kalabhras**, inaugurating the rule of the **imperial Pallavas**.
- Their core region covered **south Andhra Pradesh and north Tamil Nadu**, with **Kanchipuram (Kanchi)** as the capital.
- Throughout their reign they fought the **Chalukyas of Vatapi (Badami)** in the north and the **Cholas and Pandyas** in the south.
- Under Pallava rule **Kanchi flourished** into an important **temple town** and a hub of **trade and commerce**.
- Pallava kings assumed grand titles such as **Dharma-Maharaja**, projecting a monarchy anchored in Brahmanical kingship.

figure.alt: Map of peninsular India showing the Chalukya realm (Aihole, Badami) and the Pallava realm around Kanchipuram, with neighbouring Pandya, Ganga and Kalinga
figure.caption: Post-Gupta south India: the Chalukyas of Badami (Aihole, Badami) in the Deccan and the Pallavas around Kanchipuram, flanked by the Pandyas and Gangas.

keyPoints: Simhavishnu defeated the Kalabhras and began the imperial Pallava line.
Capital: Kanchipuram (Kanchi); core in south AP and north Tamil Nadu.
Fought the Chalukyas of Vatapi in the north; Cholas and Pandyas in the south.
Kanchi grew into a major temple town and trade centre.
Kings took the title Dharma-Maharaja.
items.mnemonic: Pallavas → capital Kanchi → temple town of the south (Mamallapuram monuments to come).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Gupta - Pallavas and Chalukyas (Emergence of the Pallavas of Kanchi)

items.title: Simhavishnu — Founder of the Imperial Pallavas
items.body:
## Simhavishnu (575–590 CE)

- **Defeated the Kalabhras** and **established the imperial Pallava dynasty**.
- Took titles such as **Avanisimha ('Lion of the Earth')**, asserting his sovereignty.
- **Patronised the Sanskrit poet Bharavi**, author of the **Kiratarjuniya**.
- His conquests laid the territorial foundation on which later Pallava greatness was built.
keyPoints: Founder of the imperial Pallavas (575–590 CE).
Defeated the Kalabhras to establish Pallava rule.
Bore the title Avanisimha ('Lion of the Earth').
Patronised the poet Bharavi, author of the Kiratarjuniya.
items.mnemonic: Simhavishnu the 'Avanisimha' → Kanchi → founder-king who crushed the Kalabhras.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Gupta - Pallavas and Chalukyas (Rulers and Contributions of the Pallavas — Simhavishnu)

items.title: Mahendravarman I — Pioneer of Rock-cut Architecture
items.body:
## Mahendravarman I (600–630 CE)

- **Expanded Pallava power** significantly and was a many-sided cultural patron.
- Took artistic titles like **Mattavilasa ('Addicted to Pleasure')** and **Chitrakarapuli ('Tiger among painters')**.
- **Introduced the Mahendra Style of rock-cut architecture** — temples cut from living rock, using **no bricks or wood**.
- Authored the **Mattavilasa Prahasana**, a Sanskrit satire.
- Was **killed by Pulakeshin II of the Chalukyas in the Battle of Pullalur**, marking the start of the long Pallava–Chalukya rivalry.
keyPoints: Reign 600–630 CE; expanded Pallava power.
Titles: Mattavilasa and Chitrakarapuli ('Tiger among painters').
Introduced the Mahendra Style — rock-cut temples with no brick or wood.
Authored the Sanskrit satire Mattavilasa Prahasana.
Killed by Pulakeshin II (Chalukya) at the Battle of Pullalur.
items.mnemonic: Mahendravarman → Kanchi → the FIRST rock-cut mandapas (Mahendra Style); lost to Pulakeshin II at Pullalur.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Gupta - Pallavas and Chalukyas (Rulers and Contributions — Mahendravarman I)

items.title: Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla) — Conqueror of Vatapi
items.body:
## Narasimhavarman I 'Mamalla' (630–668 CE)

- Regarded as the **greatest Pallava king**; took the title **Vatapikonda ('Conqueror of Vatapi')**.
- **Defeated Pulakeshin II**, king of the Chalukyas, and **destroyed Vatapi (Badami)** — avenging his father's death at Pullalur.
- **Founded Mahabalipuram (Mamallapuram)** and initiated the **Seven Rathas** (Pancha Rathas), monolithic chariot-shrines of the **Mamalla Style**.
- **Invaded Sri Lanka twice**, helping the exiled prince **Manavamma** regain his throne.
- **Hosted the Chinese traveller Hsuen Tsang (Xuanzang) at Kanchipuram in 642 CE**.

figure.alt: The monolithic Pancha Rathas (Seven Rathas) carved from granite at Mamallapuram
figure.caption: The monolithic Rathas at Mamallapuram, initiated by Narasimhavarman I — the hallmark of the Mamalla Style.

keyPoints: Greatest Pallava king (630–668 CE); title Vatapikonda.
Defeated Pulakeshin II and destroyed Vatapi (Badami).
Founded Mamallapuram; began the Seven Rathas (Mamalla Style).
Invaded Sri Lanka twice to aid the exiled prince Manavamma.
Hosted Hsuen Tsang at Kanchipuram in 642 CE.
items.mnemonic: Narasimhavarman I 'Mamalla' → Mamallapuram → the Seven Rathas; 'Vatapikonda' who razed Vatapi.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Gupta - Pallavas and Chalukyas (Rulers and Contributions — Narasimhavarman I / Mamalla)

items.title: Later Pallavas — Rajasimha and Nandivarman II
items.body:
## Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha, 695–722 CE)

- Reign marked by **peace** and a **cessation of conflicts with the Chalukyas**.
- Constructed the **Shore Temple** at Mahabalipuram and the **Kailashnath Temple** at Kanchipuram — structural temples of the **Rajasimha Style**.
- **Sent embassies to China** to strengthen foreign relations.

## Nandivarman II (736–796 CE)

- Built the **Vaikunth Perumal Temple** at Kanchi, dedicated to **Vishnu**.
- **Promoted the Bhakti Movement** through temple activities and **strengthened village autonomy**.

figure.alt: The twin-spired Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram beside the sea
figure.caption: The Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram, built by Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) — a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

keyPoints: Rajasimha (695–722 CE): peace with the Chalukyas; sent embassies to China.
Built the Shore Temple (Mahabalipuram) and Kailashnath Temple (Kanchi) — Rajasimha Style.
Nandivarman II (736–796 CE) built the Vaikunth Perumal Temple, dedicated to Vishnu.
Nandivarman II promoted the Bhakti Movement and strengthened village autonomy.
items.mnemonic: Rajasimha → Kanchi/Mahabalipuram → Shore & Kailashnath temples; Nandivarman → Vaikunth Perumal (Vishnu).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Gupta - Pallavas and Chalukyas (Rulers and Contributions — Narasimhavarman II & Nandivarman II)

items.title: Chalukyas of Badami (Vatapi) — Pulakeshin II & the Aihole Inscription
items.body:
## The Chalukyas of Vatapi (Badami)

- The **Chalukyas of Badami (Vatapi)** were the great Deccan rivals of the Pallavas, with their capital at **Badami** and a ceremonial centre at **Aihole**.
- Their greatest ruler, **Pulakeshin II**, is celebrated in the **Aihole inscription composed by his court poet Ravikirti** (a Jain), which records his conquests in refined Sanskrit.
- Pulakeshin II **checked Harshavardhana of Kanauj on the banks of the Narmada**, halting Harsha's southward advance — a landmark event of the age.
- Against the Pallavas the tide turned: Pulakeshin II **killed Mahendravarman I at Pullalur**, but was later **defeated and slain by Narasimhavarman I, who sacked Vatapi**.
- Chalukyan patronage produced the great temple complexes of **Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal**, cradles of the emerging **Vesara style**.

figure.alt: Map showing the Chalukya realm centred on Badami and Aihole in the Deccan
figure.caption: The Chalukyas of Badami (Vatapi) held the Deccan around Aihole and Badami — the Pallavas' principal northern rivals.

keyPoints: Capital Badami (Vatapi); ceremonial centre Aihole; greatest king Pulakeshin II.
Aihole inscription composed by the Jain court poet Ravikirti.
Pulakeshin II checked Harshavardhana on the Narmada.
Killed Mahendravarman I at Pullalur; later defeated and slain by Narasimhavarman I, who sacked Vatapi.
Temple complexes at Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal — nursery of the Vesara style.
items.mnemonic: Chalukyas → capital Badami (Vatapi) → Aihole & Pattadakal temples; Pulakeshin II praised by Ravikirti, stopped Harsha at the Narmada.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Gupta - Pallavas and Chalukyas (Chalukya references: Vatapi, Pulakeshin II, Battle of Pullalur; map: Aihole/Badami) with standard historical record (Aihole inscription of Ravikirti, Harsha–Narmada, Pattadakal)

items.title: Evolution of Pallava Architecture — Four Styles
items.body:
## From Rock-cut to Structural Temples

Pallava architecture evolved through four named phases and gave shape to the **Dravidian (South Indian) temple style**:

- **Mahendra Style** — the first **rock-cut temples**, using **no bricks or wood**; mandapas were pillared verandas fronting a garbhagriha (e.g. **Mamandur monuments, Trimurti Mandapa**).
- **Mamalla Style** — **Rathas (monolithic chariots)** alongside mandapas, with **lion-headed (yali) pillars** (e.g. **Seven Rathas, Varaha Mandapa, Mahishasura Mandapa**).
- **Rajasimha Style** — **structural temples** with **intricate carvings**, using **stone, wood and brick** (e.g. **Shore Temple, Kailashnath Temple**).
- **Nandivarman Style** — **smaller, less decorative** temples reflecting a **decline** (e.g. **Mukteshwar, Matangeshwar temples**).

**Style contrast:** the Pallava/Chalukya south developed the **Dravidian** (pyramidal *vimana*) style, north India the **Nagara** (curvilinear *shikhara*) style, and the Deccan a hybrid **Vesara** style.
keyPoints: Mahendra Style: first rock-cut temples, no brick/wood (Mamandur, Trimurti Mandapa).
Mamalla Style: monolithic Rathas + lion-headed pillars (Seven Rathas, Varaha Mandapa).
Rajasimha Style: elaborate structural temples in stone (Shore Temple, Kailashnath).
Nandivarman Style: smaller, less ornate temples — architectural decline.
South = Dravidian (vimana); North = Nagara (shikhara); Deccan = hybrid Vesara.
items.mnemonic: Pallava order 'Ma-Ma-Ra-Na': Mahendra (rock-cut) → Mamalla (Rathas) → Rajasimha (structural) → Nandivarman (decline).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Gupta - Pallavas and Chalukyas (Art and Architecture under the Pallavas)

items.title: Major Pallava Temples and Monuments
items.body:
## Landmark Pallava Structures

- **Shore Temple** — built by **Narasimhavarman II** at Mahabalipuram; **three shrines** dedicated to **Shiva and Vishnu**; a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.
- **Kailashnath Temple** — built by **Narasimhavarman II** at Kanchipuram; houses a **16-sided Shivalinga** and is ringed by **58 mini-shrines (devakulikas)**.
- **Seven Rathas** — initiated by **Narasimhavarman I** as early **monolithic** architecture; key rathas include **Draupadi, Dharmaraja and Bhima Rathas**.
- **Vaikunth Perumal Temple** — built by **Nandivarman II**, dedicated to **Vishnu** (shown standing, sitting and reclining); its **inscriptions record Nandivarman's ascent to power**.
- **Chittannavasal frescoes** preserve the Pallava tradition of **painting**.
keyPoints: Shore Temple (Narasimhavarman II, Mahabalipuram): three shrines, UNESCO site.
Kailashnath Temple (Narasimhavarman II, Kanchi): 16-sided Shivalinga, 58 devakulikas.
Seven Rathas (Narasimhavarman I): monolithic; Draupadi, Dharmaraja, Bhima Rathas.
Vaikunth Perumal (Nandivarman II): Vishnu in three forms; inscriptions on his accession.
Chittannavasal frescoes showcase Pallava painting.
items.mnemonic: Mahabalipuram monuments: Rathas (Narasimhavarman I) → Shore Temple (Narasimhavarman II); Kanchi → Kailashnath & Vaikunth Perumal.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Gupta - Pallavas and Chalukyas (Major Pallava Temples and Structures; Painting)

items.title: Administration under the Pallavas
items.body:
## A Monarchy Resting on Self-governing Villages

- **Form of government:** monarchy; kings assumed titles like **Dharma-Maharaja**.
- **Administrative divisions:** the empire was divided into **Kottams**, each governed by officers appointed by the king.
- **Village administration:** villages were **self-governing republics** managed by local assemblies such as the **Sabha** (for Brahmadeya villages) and the **Urar** (for ordinary villages).
- **Judiciary:** every village had a court called the **Dharmasasana** to administer justice.
- This tradition of local self-government later blossomed under the **Cholas**.
keyPoints: Monarchy; kings styled Dharma-Maharaja.
Empire divided into Kottams under royal officers.
Villages self-governed by assemblies — Sabha and Urar.
Village court called Dharmasasana dispensed justice.
Foundation for later Chola local self-government.
items.mnemonic: Pallava rule → Kanchi throne → Kottams above, Sabha/Urar villages below, Dharmasasana courts.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Gupta - Pallavas and Chalukyas (Administration under the Pallavas)

items.title: Economy under the Pallavas
items.body:
## Land, Taxes, Guilds and Grants

- **Land revenue** was the **main source of income**.
- **Taxes** were levied on **professions, marriages, salt, textiles and cattle**.
- **Agriculture** was prosperous — labourers were paid in kind, and **Hsuen Tsang** noted the region's fertile land.
- **Brahmadeya villages** (tax-free lands) were granted to Brahmins, promoting education and religion.
- A **barter system** prevailed initially, but the Pallavas later **introduced gold and silver coins** to boost trade.
- Merchants organised into guilds called **Manigramam**; **Eripatti (tank lands)** were set aside so their revenue maintained village tanks.
keyPoints: Land revenue was the primary income; taxes on professions, marriages, salt, textiles, cattle.
Prosperous agriculture; labourers paid in kind (noted by Hsuen Tsang).
Brahmadeya (tax-free) villages granted to Brahmins.
Barter gave way to gold and silver coinage to boost trade.
Manigramam = merchant guilds; Eripatti = tank lands funding village tanks.
items.mnemonic: Pallava economy: land revenue core → Brahmadeya grants → Manigramam guilds → Eripatti tank-lands.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Gupta - Pallavas and Chalukyas (Economy under the Pallavas)

items.title: Society, Religion, Literature & Decline of the Pallavas
items.body:
## Religion and the Bhakti Surge

- Pallava kings supported **Saivism and Vaishnavism**, while **Buddhism and Jainism gradually declined**.
- The **Bhakti Movement** was carried by the **Alvars (Vishnu)** and **Nayanars (Shiva)**, enriching **Tamil devotional literature** (e.g. *Nalayira Divya Prabandham*, *Tirumurai*).
- **Adi Shankaracharya** reinforced **Advaita** philosophy, further diminishing Buddhist and Jain influence.

## Arts and Literature

- **Sanskrit:** Mahendravarman I authored the **Mattavilasa Prahasana**.
- **Music and dance** were promoted (instruments: Yaazhi, Mridhangam, Murasu); **frescoes at Chittannavasal** preserve Pallava painting.

## Decline

- **Continuous wars** with the Chalukyas and Pandyas drained Pallava resources; the **Chalukyas even plundered Kanchipuram**.
- The last Pallava king, **Aparajitavarman, was defeated by the Chola king Aditya I** in the late 9th century CE — ending Pallava rule and ushering in **Chola dominance** in South India.
keyPoints: Kings favoured Saivism and Vaishnavism; Buddhism and Jainism declined.
Bhakti spread by Alvars (Vishnu) and Nayanars (Shiva) in Tamil.
Adi Shankaracharya reinforced Advaita philosophy.
Mattavilasa Prahasana (Sanskrit); Chittannavasal frescoes (painting).
Aparajitavarman, the last Pallava, was defeated by Chola Aditya I — rise of the Cholas.
items.mnemonic: Pallava twilight: Bhakti of Alvars & Nayanars at their temples → Kanchi plundered → last king Aparajitavarman falls to Chola Aditya I.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Gupta - Pallavas and Chalukyas (Society and Religion; Arts and Literature; Decline of the Pallavas)

items.title: Pulakeshin II — Diplomacy, Navy & Chalukya Precision Facts (PYQ)
items.body:
## High-Yield Chalukya Nuggets

- **Persian (Sasanian) embassy:** Pulakeshin II **exchanged embassies with the Sasanian (Persian) emperor Khusrau II (Khosrow II)** around **625 CE**. The reception of a **Persian embassy is famously depicted in a mural at Ajanta (Cave 1)**.
- **Naval power:** the Chalukyas of Badami maintained a **strong navy (about 100 ships)**, reflecting their reach along the western coast.
- **Founder & Ashvamedha:** **Pulakeshin I** founded the dynasty, fortified Vatapi (Badami) and **performed the Ashvamedha (horse sacrifice)** to proclaim sovereignty.
- **Administration contrast:** Chalukya administration was comparatively **centralised — it did NOT grant the strong village self-government** that characterised the Pallavas and, later, the Cholas (a common discrimination point).
- **Chinese testimony:** **Hiuen-Tsang visited Pulakeshin II's kingdom** and praised the just rule of the 'Maharaja of the Deccan' (whom he calls Pulakeshin).
keyPoints: Pulakeshin II exchanged embassies with the Sasanian (Persian) emperor Khusrau II (c. 625 CE); the Persian embassy is depicted in an Ajanta Cave 1 mural.
The Badami Chalukyas kept a strong navy of about 100 ships.
Pulakeshin I, the founder, fortified Vatapi and performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Chalukya administration was relatively centralised — unlike the strong village autonomy of the Pallavas/Cholas.
Hiuen-Tsang visited and praised Pulakeshin II's Deccan kingdom.
items.source: standard historical record — Aihole inscription, Ajanta Cave 1 Persian-embassy mural, Hiuen-Tsang's account of the Deccan
